title: When Certainty Is Noise Date Published: June 3, 2026 Original URL: https://gregmckeown.com
author: Greg McKeown
summary: McKeown uses the 1983 Soviet nuclear near-miss — when Lieutenant Colonel Stanislav Petrov refused to forward a computer's confident alert of five incoming American missiles, reasoning that a real first strike would be massive rather than limited — as an illustration of the signal vs. noise distinction in leadership judgment. Petrov's genius was not that he ignored the system but that he interrogated it: he did not ask only 'what does the system say?' but 'what does it mean?' — and in the gap between those two questions, with only minutes to decide, he exercised the judgment that prevented nuclear war. McKeown's concept of the 'Signalist' is a leader who does not simply react to messages but asks about their meaning — who recognizes that high confidence in a system is not the same as accuracy, and that false certainty is a failure mode distinct from false information. The article generalizes from the geopolitical to the organizational and interpersonal: a terse email becomes proof of anger, a missed response becomes proof of being ignored, a poor result becomes proof of failure — each of these is a confident system reading that a Signalist pauses to interrogate. McKeown frames this as the core discipline of what he calls being a Signalist: not skepticism about all information but the habit of pausing to ask 'what does this message actually mean?' before allowing confidence in a signal to trigger an irreversible response. The Petrov example is powerful precisely because the stakes were maximal and the time pressure was acute: the habits of signal-interpretation that serve leaders in ordinary decisions are the same ones that, under extreme pressure, determine whether irreversible actions are taken on false information.
points: Confidence and accuracy are independent dimensions: the Soviet early-warning system was simultaneously highly confident and completely wrong — and the organization's entire decision architecture treated confidence as a reliable proxy for accuracy, which is the failure mode Petrov's judgment corrected.

The Signalist's discipline requires habituating a pause between 'what does the system/data/message say?' and 'what does it mean?' — a tiny cognitive gap that, practiced consistently, prevents the most costly interpretive errors in leadership.

The social version of this error (terse email = anger, missed response = being ignored) is particularly treacherous because it involves people rather than machines: social pattern recognition is fast, confident, and systematically susceptible to projection and confirmation bias.

Petrov's reasoning process illustrates exactly what the pause looks like: he didn't know the system was wrong, but he noticed an inconsistency between the system's confidence and the pattern he would expect from a genuine first strike — it wasn't proof, it was pattern, and that was enough to pause before forwarding an irreversible alert.

McKeown's framing of this as a learnable discipline (the Signalist identity) rather than a fixed cognitive trait means it can be cultivated: the practice is simply to delay action on high-confidence signals long enough to ask what the signal actually means in context.
quotes: A Signalist doesn't just react to a message. A Signalist asks what it means.

Then the alarm sounded. A red warning flashed across the screen: LAUNCH DETECTED. According to the computer, the United States had fired an intercontinental ballistic missile at the Soviet Union. Then another. Then another. Soon, the system declared that five nuclear missiles were inbound. The message was clear. The system was confident. Protocol demanded action. This is what noise looks like at scale.

Petrov had only minutes to decide whether to transmit that message to the highest levels of Soviet leadership, where it could trigger a retaliatory strike and a chain reaction no one could stop. He looked at the screen. The warning was bright, confident, definitive. And then he did something extraordinary. He paused.

He did not ask only, 'What does the system say?' He asked, 'What does it mean?' If the United States were launching a first strike, why would it send only five missiles? A real first strike would likely be massive. It wasn't proof. It was pattern.

Petrov's genius was not that he ignored the system. It was that he interpreted it. He did not have perfect information. He did not have more authority than the system. He had one power: the ability to ask what the message meant. And that was enough.

We do this in smaller ways all the time. A terse email becomes proof someone is angry. A missed response becomes proof we are being ignored. A poor result becomes proof the strategy has failed. We treat our interpretation as signal. But many of these responses are noise — confident, compelling, and wrong.
